title: Silent final consonants
summary: Many final consonants are silent in ordinary speech, but spelling still records them.
full_explanation: Final -s on plurals and the -ent of ils/elles verbs are usually silent. Liaison can make a silent letter audible before a vowel. Spelling and sound diverge — trust both.

bullets: ils/elles -ent silent: ils parlent ≈ il parle
Liaison: you may hear the consonant before a vowel (ils‿ont)
Write the letters even when you don’t say them

deepDive.whyItMatters: If you pronounce every letter, you sound non-native and mis-hear plurals. If you drop letters in writing, verbs look singular. Lesson 1.3 marks silent segments visually — match ear and eye.

sections.heading: Plural -s / -x
sections.body: les, des, mes, vos — the -s is silent unless liaison. Les amis can sound like lé-z-ami.

sections.heading: Verb ending -ent
sections.body: Ils habitent, elles parlent — write -ent, say nothing extra. This is not the adverb ending -ment (lentement), which is pronounced.

sections.heading: Other silent finals
sections.body: Many words end in silent -t, -d, -s, -x: petit, grand, bas. Exceptions exist (sac — c is heard). Learn word by word.

sections.heading: Liaison vs silence
sections.body: Silent letter can wake up before a vowel: vous‿êtes, ils‿ont, les‿amis. Not every boundary is a liaison — listen for models in dialogue.

pronunciationNotes: Train pairs: il parle / ils parlent (same sound, different spelling).
Use lesson X-Ray / silent marks when available.

exercise.statement: The -ent ending in ils parlent is usually silent in speech.
exercise.explanation: Yes — write -ent, don’t pronounce an extra syllable.
